turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come through, we'll grab your obs before the doctor gets free. Shoes off for the scales if the knee lets you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, I'll try. I don't know if I can reach the laces, that's half the problem.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I've got them. We were circling the car park for ages, the machine wouldn't take my card.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Ninety-four... sorry, ninety-one point six kilos. Blood pressure's one fifty-two over eighty-eight, pulse seventy-six. Any allergies I should put on the chart?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I'm allergic to.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Never has been, not to medicines anyway. The car park's a rort, two dollars for twenty minutes.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, this thing's frozen again. Righto. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the right knee. Going down the stairs, it really grabs.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Say that again? I clicked the wrong letter. Stairs, was it?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, down the stairs. And the right one wakes me at night. I don't know, doctor, it just aches and I have to shift it.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long's all that been going on?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks... well, actually, no. More like two months. Since it got cold.
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She won't come down our front steps to the shops anymore. I do the bread run.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): When it wakes you, is it every night?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Most nights. I don't know how many times, I lose count.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does the knee swell up, or give way under you?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): It doesn't give way. Swelling, I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The right knee looks a bit puffy by the evening sometimes. She tells me not to fuss.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or feeling crook otherwise?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I feel fine apart from the knee.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): What are you using on it?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): That gel from the chemist, for the knee. Voltaren, the diclofenac one. I rub it on twice a day.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Not every morning, though. Some days it stays in the drawer and she forgets.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I try to remember. I don't know, doctor, I think I mostly do.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, gel twice a day, yes? And anything by mouth from the chemist?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Morning and night when I remember, yeah. And sometimes the tablets by mouth, the diclofenac ones, fifty milligrams... no, twenty-five. The box says twenty-five. One for the knee when it's really bad, two or three times a week.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Two or three times a week, not every day?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Not every day. I don't know, doctor, it depends how the stairs were.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any stomach problems with those? Ulcers, reflux, anything like that?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No stomach problems.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She has tea and a biscuit around four. We're trying to cut the biscuits, with the weight and all. Her sister rang this morning about a cruise, of all things.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nurse, what was that weight again? The obs have dropped off my screen.
[SEG0033] person_1 (NURSE): Ninety-one point six kilograms. Blood pressure one fifty-two on eighty-eight, pulse seventy-six.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's a fair load on a sore knee. Been heavier lately, do you reckon?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. I never get on the scales at home.
[SEG0036] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Under ninety at some point, but I couldn't tell you when. Doesn't matter.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll just bend it. Tender along the inside of the right knee, and there's crepitus as it flexes. No fluid in the joint that I can feel.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow, yep, that's the bit. Down the stairs is the worst of it.

[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): I think this is osteoarthritis in the right knee, with the stair pain and the night aching. I'll refer you to physio this week, and I'll start naproxen, two hundred and fifty milligrams twice a day.
[SEG0040] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's already swallowing those chemist tablets, though. And she was up with heartburn last night, burning in the chest after tea.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yeah. I do get heartburn. I said no stomach trouble but the burning's there most evenings, a few weeks now. I don't know if it's the tablets.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, run the heartburn past me again? I was typing.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Most evenings, after tea. A few weeks. I don't know, doctor, it's just burning.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right, that changes the plan. Scratch the naproxen, I won't prescribe it, and I want you to stop the diclofenac tablets from the chemist. Keep using the gel on the knee.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Stop them altogether? Even the twenty-five ones?

[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, no more of those tablets. And I was going to book the physio outright, but I'm not deciding that today. We might send you to physio, or we might do a cortisone injection into the knee if it's still waking you. I won't arrange either one now.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She wanted something quicker than exercises. Those stairs at home are steep, no rail on the bottom bit.

[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Both options stay open. Come back in three weeks and we'll choose. Meanwhile ease off the biscuits, even a couple of kilos would help that knee, and you can grab some Gaviscon from the chemist for the heartburn if you like.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Three weeks is a while if I'm up all night.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the night pain gets properly worse, ring and we'll see you sooner. Otherwise three weeks. Sorry, the screen just blinked, yes, three weeks.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. Three weeks, and the tablets go.
[SEG0052] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll put the tablet box in the bin and leave the gel by the kettle so she sees it.
[SEG0053] person_1 (NURSE): I can book that three-week review at the desk when you head out.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ta. No x-ray for now, I don't think we need one.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): I still don't know about a needle in the knee. Injections make me go funny.
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): You don't have to decide anything today. We'll talk it through properly next visit.
[SEG0057] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Come on then, shoes. Mind you don't twist on the way out.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Thanks. I think that's all, I don't know what else to say.
[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's plenty. See you in three weeks, unless you ring sooner.
[SEG0060] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We'll be there. Say thanks, love, she already did. Off we go.

omissions.text: No stomach problems/ulcers/reflux was initially denied when asked about diclofenac side effects, but this was later corrected: the patient does have heartburn/burning in the chest most evenings for a few weeks, possibly related to the tablets.
Naproxen 250 mg twice a day was initially proposed, then explicitly cancelled and not prescribed because of the heartburn.
Physiotherapy was initially said to be referred this week, but this plan was reversed: the doctor decided not to arrange physiotherapy today.
No X-ray for now; the doctor said they do not think one is needed.
The patient denied feeling unwell otherwise: 'I feel fine apart from the knee.'
The patient was unsure whether the knee swells ('I don't know'), rather than personally confirming swelling.
The patient was unsure/reluctant about a knee injection, saying injections make her 'go funny'; the doctor said no decision was needed today and they would discuss it next visit.
